extracted.intended_audience: scientific inquirers, students of philosophy of science, and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating scientific hypotheses, empirical laws, and progressive effects — when inferences from observation are legitimate, what counts as an empirical law, and the limits of inductive methods. Aimed at applying methods of induction/deduction in natural philosophy and the sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate inference to past causes (geology/judicial analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimate operation of inferring from an observed effect the existence, in time past, of a cause similar to that by which we know it to be produced in all cases in which we have actual experience of its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when the effect closely resembles effects known to be produced by a particular cause and 'no other known cause could have generated the effects shown to have been produced.' Examples: geological inference from deposits resembling those formed by water or fire; judicial inference from corpse indications. Do not treat such inferences as speculative hypotheses if they rest on 'uniformities ascertained by a perfect induction' and the agents and laws involved are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conjectural hypotheses from legitimate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between inventing agencies to account for classes of phenomena, and endeavoring, in conformity with known laws, to conjecture what former collocations of known agents may have given birth to individual facts still in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat invented agencies or properties (unknown substances or laws) as hypotheses or conjectures; treat reconstructions using known agents and laws (e.g., geological reconstructions, Laplace-style accounts) as inductive inference. Remain cautious: even inductive reconstructions may be less secure than direct geological inferences if they require assuming long-range temporal constancy of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical law (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical Laws are those uniformities which observation or experiment has shown to exist, but on which inquirers hesitate to rely in cases varying much from those actually observed; it is implied that it is not an ultimate law, but a derivative law, the derivation of which is not yet known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat observed regularities as provisional 'empirical laws' until they are explained deductively (i.e., their 'why' is given). Examples listed: local tidal laws, weather successional rules, exceptions to thermal expansion, laws about breeds improved by crossing, etc. Expect that empirical laws require further resolution into simpler laws and that their limits must be established by such analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of empirical laws (time, place, circumstance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time and place in which they have been found true by observation; and not merely the limits of time and place, but of time, place, and circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend empirical generalizations beyond the conditions of observation without further evidence or deductive explanation. Examples: the proposition that coal-beds rest on certain strata on Earth cannot be assumed to hold on the moon because collocations of causes may differ. Empirical laws require actual trial to test their applicability in new circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone is insufficient to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization amounts to more than an empirical law when the only proof on which it rests is that of the Method of Agreement; by that method alone we never can arrive at causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the Method of Agreement only ascertains circumstances common to all observed cases; this aggregate includes the true cause plus collateral uniformities and co-existing effects. Avoid treating such commonalities as definitive proof of causation; further methods are required to isolate causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for Method of Difference or deductive explanation to elevate an empirical law
rubrics_metrics.description: Results obtained by the Method of Agreement (and therefore almost all truths obtained by simple observation without experiment) must be considered empirical laws until either confirmed by the Method of Difference, or explained deductively; in other words, accounted for a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To move from empirical law to causal law, pursue controlled contrasts (Method of Difference) or deduce the law from more ultimate laws of causation. Confirmation by experiment or theoretical derivation provides the 'why' and establishes the law's wider authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes and progressive effects (continuing causes produce accumulated effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause which continues in action must on a strict analysis be considered as a number of causes exactly similar, successively introduced, and producing by their combination the sum of the effects which they would severally produce if they acted singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand progressive phenomena (rusting, continuous gravitational acceleration) as the sum of successive increments; such cases are amenable to mathematical/deductive treatment (differential calculus). When analyzing progressive effects, consider proximate vs remote causes (e.g., motion at an instant is caused by motion at the preceding instant rather than by the original impulse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of progressive change in causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cause does not merely continue in action, but undergoes during the same time a progressive change in those of its circumstances which contribute to determine the effect, the quantities added are unequal and the quality may be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model such cases as double series: accumulation from continuance and variation from progressive change. Examples: seasonal temperature increases (continuance of solar heating plus the sun's changing altitude) and planetary motion (central force and acquired motion both permanent and progressive). Account for interactions and reactions between effects and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying authority of empirical laws depending on derivability
rubrics_metrics.description: These empirical laws may be of greater or less authority, according as there is reason to presume that they are resolvable into laws only, or into laws and collocations together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate strength of an empirical law by assessing whether it plausibly derives from ultimate laws (stronger) or from particular collocations of agents (weaker). Example: growth stages of organisms likely reflect progressive effects from common causes (stronger); order of geological strata likely depends on collocations (weaker). Use this evaluation to judge how far to generalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in assuming constancy of laws over deep time
rubrics_metrics.description: There would still be a much greater chance of error in assuming that the existing laws of nature are the same which existed at the origin of the solar system, than in merely presuming (with geologists) that those laws have lasted through a few revolutions and transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing historical/deductive accounts (e.g., Laplace's nebular hypothesis), avoid undue confidence in extending present laws indefinitely backward; quantify uncertainty and prefer explanations that rely on shorter-range constancies when possible. Recognize that even deductively plausible scenarios may be speculative if they depend on long-term invariance of laws.
